title: Turn Your Mission Into A Moat
excerptForBlog:
My view is that the best future will come from a major expansion of OpenAI. Our goal and mission are fundamentally correct, and that will increasingly be a superpower as AGI grows near.

Our fundraising conversations show that Ilya and I are able to convince reputable people that AGI can really happen in the next <=10 years, there's appetite for donations from those people, and there's very large appetite for investments from those people.

Over the next 3 years, we must build 3 things: Custom AI hardware, a massive AI data center, and the best software team, mixing between algorithm development, public demonstrations, and safety. We also have identified a small but finite number of limitations in today's deep learning which are barriers to learning from human levels of experience. And we believe we uniquely are on trajectory to solving safety (at least in broad strokes) in the next three years.

Our biggest tool is the moral high ground. To retain this, we must try our best to remain a non-profit — AI is going to shake up the fabric of society, and our fiduciary duty should be to humanity. We need to communicate a 'better red than dead' outlook — we're trying to build safe AGI, and we're not willing to destroy the world in a down-to-the-wire race to do so. We must also engage with government to provide trusted, unbiased policy advice, and be perceived as a place that provides public good to the research community.

lessonTitle: Turn Your Mission Into A Moat
pullQuote: When you can't outspend competitors, out-trust them — moral high ground is a strategic asset, not a slogan.
situation: On January 31, 2018, OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman wrote an internal strategy memo laying out a three-year build plan. The memo surfaced in the Musk v. Altman litigation. At stake: how OpenAI would compete for talent, capital, and credibility against better-resourced commercial rivals.
insight:
Brockman's sharpest move is hiding in plain sight. He calls non-profit status 'our biggest tool' and frames it explicitly as 'the moral high ground' — something to be retained strategically, not just honored ethically. This is **positioning as a moat**. Commercial AI labs can outspend OpenAI on hardware and salaries, but they can't easily claim the same fiduciary duty to humanity. Brockman is betting that as AGI approaches, that credibility gap becomes a durable advantage — with donors, with policy makers, and with the researchers who want to work somewhere they trust.

The memo also reveals a resource-stacking logic: it lists three simultaneous build targets — custom hardware, a major data center, and a top software team — while noting that fundraising conversations show 'very large appetite for investments.' Brockman is not treating the non-profit mission as a constraint on growth. He's using it as the pitch that unlocks the capital to fund aggressive scaling.
application: If your company has a genuine mission constraint — a commitment that limits what you'll do — stop treating it as a liability and test whether it's an asset. Map who values that constraint: investors, regulators, recruits, partners. Then make that constraint visible and specific in your fundraising and hiring materials, the way Brockman does with the phrase 'better red than dead.' A credible limit can attract the right stakeholders faster than a promise of unlimited upside.
